title: Food Forest Design
narration:
Build a living food system in layers.

Grow food from tall canopy down to root crops.

Use vertical space, soil life, shade, and moisture together.

Learn how to design and establish a food forest for your farm.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Why This Matters
narration:
A food forest can give food from many levels of the same piece of land.

It can use light and moisture that a single crop would leave unused.

The first years need steady work.

Later, shade, leaf-fall mulch, and mixed roots help the system care for itself.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Learning Outcomes
narration:
Name the seven layers of a food forest.

Choose species that match your frost zone, rainfall, and humidity.

Plan a planting sequence for a 500m² plot.

Know why pioneers come first, and when lower layers and climbers should follow.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: The Forest Uses Every Layer
narration:
An indigenous forest fills the space from the highest branches to the roots.

Different plants use the light and moisture available at their level.

A food forest copies this pattern with productive species.

The result is not one crop in one row, but many useful layers growing together.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: The Seven Layers Working Together
narration:
Read the planting downwards, from the tall canopy to the roots.

Climbers use the open vertical space between the layers.

One piece of ground, working at every level.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: The Seven Layers
narration:
Tall canopy grows at 10m+.

Sub-canopy grows from 4–8m, while shrubs grow from 1–3m.

Herbaceous plants stay under 1m.

Ground cover protects the soil, root crops grow below, and climbers use vertical space.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: A Highveld Example
narration:
The canopy might hold a large Wild Fig or pecan.

The sub-canopy can carry lemon, naartjie, and black mulberry.

Cape gooseberry and Wild Medlar fit the shrub layer.

Vegetables, wild garlic, sweet potato, and granadilla fill the lower layers and vertical spaces.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: From Establishment to Self-Care
narration:
The first two to three years need real establishment work.

Weeds compete strongly with herbaceous plants and ground cover on open, sunlit soil.

By year three to five, the canopy closes.

Shade and deep leaf-fall mulch reduce evaporation, while mixed roots hold more soil moisture.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Choose for Your Region
narration:
Match each species to your region before planting.

Know your rainfall, minimum winter temperature, frost frequency, and summer humidity.

A mango that thrives on the KZN coast dies at the first Highveld frost.

A quince needing winter chill won't fruit in a frost-free coastal belt.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: Match the Species to the Climate
narration:
Climate decides which species belong.

On the Highveld, choose cold-tolerant trees and shrubs; on the KZN coast and Lowveld, choose warm-climate species.

Match every plant to your site.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Highveld Food Forest Choices
narration:
Highveld canopy choices include pecan, walnut, and indigenous fig.

Apple, pear, plum, black mulberry, and loquat can form the sub-canopy.

Shrubs include rosemary, Wild Medlar, Cape gooseberry, and Barbados cherry.

Do not plant from a list alone. Check the conditions on your own land first.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: KZN Coast, Lowveld, and Limpopo
narration:
KZN coast and Lowveld can suit mango, avocado, and Natal Mahogany.

Banana, pawpaw, litchi, and Wild Fig belong in the sub-canopy.

Barbados cherry and Wild Dagga belong in the shrub layer.

In Limpopo Lowveld, Marula, Mopane, and baobab may be appropriate.

These trees are edible and culturally significant.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Indigenous Species Build the Ecosystem
narration:
Aim for at least 30% indigenous species throughout the food forest.

They support the birds and insects that make the system work.

These visitors provide pest control, pollination, and seed dispersal.

That support makes the food forest more resilient than a collection of fruit trees alone.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Plant in Sequence
narration:
A food forest is planted in sequence, not all at once.

First come nitrogen-fixing pioneers to improve soil and offer shade.

Then come the main canopy and sub-canopy fruit trees.

Lower layers follow when the canopy gives some protection.

Climbers and ground covers come last.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: From Bare Ground to Food Forest
narration:
Sheet-mulch first.

Pioneers build soil while fruit trees establish.

As shelter grows, plant the lower layers, ground covers, and climbers.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Year One on a 500m² Plot
narration:
Sheet-mulch with cardboard and 20cm of wood chips.

The cardboard smothers existing grass while it decomposes and feeds soil organisms.

Plant nitrogen-fixing pioneers at 2m spacing.

Start a nursery so more plants are ready for the next stage.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Years Two to Four
narration:
In year two, plant the main fruit trees.

Interplant comfrey and wild garlic beneath them.

During years three to four, thin the pioneers because they would otherwise compete too strongly for light with the maturing fruit trees.

Use the pioneer cuttings as mulch, so their soil-building work continues.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Plant With the Rain
narration:
Plant at the start of the rainy season.

Let the rain do the establishment watering.

Never plant into dry soil.

Transplant shock plus drought stress rarely allows a young plant to recover.

By year five, a 500m² Highveld food forest can produce real harvests with minimal outside inputs.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Field Assignment
narration:
Draw your own food forest in layers.

Mark the canopy, sub-canopy, shrub, herbaceous, ground cover, root crop, and climber spaces.

Write down your frost zone, rainfall, minimum winter temperature, frost frequency, and summer humidity.

Choose only species from this lesson that match your conditions.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Field Action
narration:
Choose a plot and inspect the soil before planting.

Plan the sheet mulch with cardboard and wood chips.

Prepare your pioneer plants and nursery.

When the rainy season starts, plant the first sequence and watch which layers need the most care.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Introduction to Permaculture
narration:
Before you dig anything, it helps to know how the decisions get made.

This module is the foundation for everything else in the course. Three ethics, a set of design principles, and one simple way to organise your land.

None of it needs money. All of it changes where you put things, and how far you walk every day.

[pause]

Think about your own plot. Which part of it do you visit most often?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Why This Matters
narration:
A good design saves work before you pick up a spade.

Most of the effort on a smallholding is not planting or harvesting. It is walking, carrying and fixing what was put in the wrong place.

Permaculture is a way of deciding where things go, so the land works with you instead of against you.

[pause]

Think of one job on your farm that takes longer than it should. Where does the time actually go?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Learning Outcomes
narration:
By the end of this module you will be able to do three things.

Name the three ethics, and use them to settle a decision that has no obvious answer.

Name the design principles that matter most on your land, and say why.

Sketch your zones and your sectors on one sheet of paper.

[pause]

That sketch is the skeleton of every plan you make after this.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Earth Care
narration:
The first ethic is Earth Care.

It means treating soil, water, plants and animals as living systems to protect, not resources to use up.

A system you use up stops paying you. A system you protect keeps paying you.

[pause]

Look at one patch of bare soil on your land. Is anything protecting it right now?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: People Care
narration:
The second ethic is People Care.

Your family's needs come first, then your community's.

A farmer who sells every egg and every vegetable, and keeps nothing back for the family table, is skipping People Care.

The farm is meant to feed the household that runs it.

[pause]

What comes off your land that your own family never eats?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Fair Share
narration:
The third ethic is Fair Share.

Take only what you need, and return the surplus to the system — seeds, food, water, knowledge.

A farmer who sells all his surplus mielies and keeps nothing back for compost or for seed is breaking this one. Nothing goes back.

A community that fences off a shared spring is breaking it too.

[pause]

What does your land get back from you each season?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: One Decision, Three Ethics
narration:
A borehole is producing more water than your household needs.

You could keep it closed. You could open it to everyone and watch the level drop.

Sharing access with your neighbours while you monitor the water table serves all three at once. People Care and Fair Share in the sharing. Earth Care in the monitoring.

[pause]

The other choices each serve one ethic and ignore the rest.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: When There Is No Rulebook
narration:
This is what the ethics are actually for.

A neighbour asks to graze cattle after a drought. A flood damages your swales. Nobody has written down the answer.

The ethics let you decide without waiting for permission, and explain the decision afterwards.

[pause]

Build these three into how you think before you build anything on the ground.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Twelve Principles
narration:
Bill Mollison and David Holmgren distilled permaculture into twelve design principles.

You do not need all twelve to start. Three of them do most of the work on a South African smallholding.

Observe and interact. Catch and store energy. Use edges and value the marginal.

[pause]

We will take those three one at a time.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Observe and Interact
narration:
Watch your land through a full season before you commit to major earthworks.

One storm shows you one moment. A full wet season shows you the pattern — where water runs, where it pools, where it never reaches.

That pattern is what a swale has to match. Dig before you know it and you have moved a great deal of soil into the wrong place.

[pause]

Where does water leave your land? Do you actually know, or are you guessing?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Catch and Store Energy
narration:
Harvest rain, sun and biomass before they leave your property.

Every one of those arrives free and leaves free. Water runs off, leaves blow away, sun falls on bare ground.

Catching them is almost always cheaper than buying the same thing later.

[pause]

Name one thing that arrives on your land free and leaves again without being used.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Use Edges and Value the Marginal
narration:
The edge is where two things meet — a fence line, a stream bank, the strip beside a path.

Edges are often the most productive ground you have, and they are usually the ground nobody has planned.

Look at what already grows well along yours. That is the land telling you something.

[pause]

Which edge on your plot is doing nothing at the moment?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: Diversity Against One Bad Day
narration:
A monoculture maize field can be wiped out by one hailstorm. A mixed planting rarely is.

That is the principle "use and value diversity", and it is insurance you plant rather than buy.

Two others worth knowing: produce no waste, so scraps become compost and compost becomes soil. And use small and slow solutions — a bucket can irrigate a bed with no electricity at all.

[pause]

What would one bad day cost you right now?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Integrate Rather Than Segregate
narration:
Put each element where it works for its neighbours.

A garden, fruit trees and a chicken run arranged so the chickens rotate through the beds after harvest is integration. The chickens clean up pests and add fertility instead of sitting idle in a fixed pen.

The same three things, fenced apart, do only their own job.

[pause]

Pick two or three principles that speak to your biggest problem and apply them hard. The rest become obvious as you go.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Zones: Organising by How Often You Visit
narration:
Zones run from 0 to 5, and they are about your feet, not your fences.

Zone 0 is the house. Zone 1, right outside the kitchen door, holds what you pick daily — herbs and salad greens.

Zone 2 is the main garden and the chicken run, visited once or twice a day. Zone 3 is the main field, visited weekly.

[pause]

Zone 4 is semi-wild — fruit trees and fodder that need occasional attention. Zone 5 is left wild.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Why Zone 1 Is Not Negotiable
narration:
Herbs need daily picking to stay productive.

Plant them in Zone 3, out in the main field, and the walk is long enough that the daily visit stops happening. The herbs bolt, or they are simply neglected.

Nothing is wrong with the plant or the soil. The plant was put where your feet do not go.

[pause]

What is currently planted further from your door than it deserves?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Zones Plan Your Labour
narration:
This is the point of the whole exercise.

Zones do not organise space. They organise effort — the walking, the carrying and the checking that fills a real day.

The more often something needs you, the closer it lives. That one rule cuts real hours over a season.

[pause]

Stand at your kitchen door. What can you reach without thinking about it?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Sectors: The Energies Arriving From Outside
narration:
Zones come from inside your land. Sectors come from outside it.

Sun, wind, rain, flood and fire all arrive across your boundary whether you plan for them or not.

A Lowveld farm facing north-west gets hot dry berg winds in August. A KwaZulu-Natal farm has a summer rain sector from the north-east.

[pause]

Which direction does the weather that damages you come from?
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: A Windbreak Belongs On The Wind Side
narration:
A Highveld farm gets hot, dry north-westerly winds in August.

The windbreak goes on the north-west boundary, standing between the wind and the crops.

That is all a windbreak does — it stands between the energy and the thing the energy would damage. Put it anywhere else and it is just a row of trees.

[pause]

The same logic places a firebreak, and it places your tender crops out of a frost pocket.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Sketch It And You Have A Design
narration:
Draw your boundary. Mark the house. Draw the rings outward by how often you visit.

Then draw arrows in from outside for sun, wind, fire and water.

That sheet of paper is the skeleton of your design. Everything else in this course hangs on it.

[pause]

It does not need to be neat. It needs to be true.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Field Assignment
narration:
Sketch your own zones and sectors on one sheet of paper.

Mark Zone 0 and Zone 1 first, then work outward as far as your land goes.

Add an arrow for each energy that arrives from outside, and label where it comes from.

Photograph the sketch.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Field Action
narration:
Walk out and check your sketch against the ground.

Stand at the kitchen door and count what is really in Zone 1 today.

Find one thing planted further away than how often you use it, and write down where it should move to.

Then ask one older neighbour which direction the worst wind comes from, and compare their answer with your arrow.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Market Gardening & Community
narration:
Your garden gives food, income, and useful knowledge.

This module shows how to keep records, sell surplus, and build local food networks.

The aim is a farm that feeds the household and works as a small, clear economy.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Why This Matters
narration:
Most smallholders undersell what their farms produce because they do not write it down.

A tomato, an egg, or a bundle of morogo can go to the family, a customer, a neighbour, or compost.

When you record each one, you can see what your land and labour are really doing.

That clear picture helps you protect household food and make better business choices.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Learning Outcomes
narration:
By the end, you can record harvests and where they go.

You can work out the true cost of production before setting a price.

You can match surplus to a suitable customer or selling channel.

You can build a local network for seeds, tools, skills, and food.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: What the Farm Record Shows
narration:
The record follows each harvest to family food, sales, gifts, or compost.

Read across the season to see the farm as an economy before making a business decision.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Record Every Harvest
narration:
Write down every harvest as it happens.

Record kilograms of tomatoes, dozens of eggs, and bundles of morogo, then note where each went.

Use the same simple habit for food kept at home, produce sold, produce gifted, and produce composted.

Do not rely on memory at the end of the season.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Let One Season Answer Questions
narration:
One season of records answers practical questions.

Which crops give the best yield per bed? Which return the most for each hour of work?

Which crops use more seeds, water, and compost than they return?

The record also shows which months leave the household buying food.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Find the True Cost
narration:
Before you set a selling price, add the real costs.

Include seeds, water, compost, and an honest hourly rate for your own labour.

If tomatoes cost R18/kg to produce, selling them at R15/kg loses money on every kilogram.

Raise the price to at least R18/kg, cut input costs, or move labour to better crops.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Plant for the Food Gap
narration:
A record can show a food gap before the next season begins.

If vegetables are short in June and July, plan cold-tolerant winter crops in March-April.

This is not guessing. The dates come from your own farm record.

Planting for the gap can help the household eat more of its own food.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: Where Surplus Can Go
narration:
Surplus can leave the farm through a roadside stall, a group delivery to a shop, or a box delivered to a household.

The arrows show each route.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Know Your Customer
narration:
Know your customer before you sell.

A formal farmers’ market may pay a premium price, but it demands registration and a consistent weekly supply.

An informal market or taxi-rank stall pays less, but asks nothing in return.

A school or clinic may pay below retail and give a stable order.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Keep More Through Direct Selling
narration:
Direct selling can keep the full price with you.

Door-to-door sales, a WhatsApp order group, and weekly deliveries remove the middleman.

A box scheme works differently: customers subscribe to a regular vegetable box.

Their commitment gives you predictable income and helps you plan production around real demand.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Plan Around Box Customers
narration:
A box scheme can suit a garden of 200 to 500m².

Ten regular box customers can provide meaningful monthly income.

The important value is not only the price per kilogram.

You know in advance what customers expect, so you grow for real demand instead of growing speculatively.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Match the Channel to Your Supply
narration:
If production changes from week to week, do not promise a fixed box.

Sell what you have through an informal market or to neighbours with no fixed commitment.

Choose a price that covers the true cost of production.

Trust through farm visits and an honest reputation matters more than expensive organic certification for most smallholders.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: How Neighbours Strengthen a Harvest
narration:
One farm can produce food.

A group can share seed, tools, skills, and transport.

Separate growers become a stronger local food network, with each household contributing what it can.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Save Seed Together
narration:
A seed swap between five neighbours can turn five households’ seed diversity into twenty-five.

If five smallholders each save three tomato varieties alone, or each saves two varieties for the group, collective saving gives better seed.

Specialising means more attention to isolation, selection, and storage.

The whole group receives stronger seed without every farmer doing every task alone.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Share Expensive Tools
narration:
Tool sharing puts expensive equipment within reach of the group.

A water pump or grain mill may be beyond one household’s budget.

Shared use spreads the value across the group and helps each farm do work it could not do alone.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Sell Locally to Reduce Loss
narration:
About a third of fresh fruit and vegetables grown by smallholders is lost between harvest and sale.

Poor transport, packaging, and storage delays cause much of this loss.

Selling within walking distance removes most of it. If a formal market is 60km away, moving 50kg of beans sold at R8/kg can cost R150.

A WhatsApp group or community market removes that transport cost and may reach R10/kg.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Share Skills as Well as Things
narration:
A farmer who has mastered grafting or managed fungal disease in humid KZN summers can teach ten neighbours.

That lesson may change ten farms, not just one.

Monthly skills swaps build knowledge more durably than a single expert consultation.

Document what you learn, then pass it on so the knowledge stays in the community.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Field Assignment: Make a Farm Record
narration:
Use headings for harvest, where it went, costs, and labour.

Record every kilogram, dozen, or bundle as it leaves the farm.

Include food kept by the household, produce sold, produce gifted, and produce composted.

At the end of one season, identify a crop that returns well and a month when the household buys food.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Field Action: Use the Record
narration:
Choose one real selling decision from your farm.

If a product costs more to produce than its selling price, raise the price, cut input costs, or shift labour to a better crop.

If a food gap appears in June and July, plan cold-tolerant winter crops in March-April.

Then talk with neighbours about one local sale, seed swap, tool share, or skills swap.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Plant Selection and Guilds
narration:
Healthy farms do not depend on a single plant doing every job.

Choose plants that feed the soil, protect crops, cover the ground, and give food.

This is the work of plant selection and plant guilds.

The aim is a strong system for South African conditions.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Why Plant Guilds Matter
narration:
When soil is tired, crops struggle to grow.

Nitrogen is what most limits growth in degraded South African soils.

Plants can take nitrogen from the air, return minerals through mulch, and call helpful insects into the garden.

Together, they support the crops around them.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Learning Outcomes
narration:
By the end, you can explain how legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen through rhizobia in root nodules.

You can choose mulch plants and use chop and drop to return material to the soil surface.

You can plan flowering plants and wild garlic for biological pest management.

You can build a mango guild with each plant given a clear job.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: How Legumes Feed the Soil
narration:
Most plants need nitrogen for strong growth.

Legumes partner with soil bacteria called rhizobia.

The bacteria pull nitrogen from the air and fix it in nodules on the roots.

When roots die back, or the plant is cut, that nitrogen becomes available to neighbouring plants.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: Roots That Feed the Soil
narration: Look at the roots below the soil. Small nodules show where rhizobia fix nitrogen, helping a living legume feed the soil around it.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Nitrogen-Fixing Trees
narration:
Useful nitrogen-fixing trees include Senegalia, formerly Acacia, species and relatives like flat-crown, Albizia adianthifolia.

Tagasaste suits the Western Cape and highland zones.

It self-seeds readily, so plant it with care near untransformed land.

Sesbania sesban suits warm, moist KZN coastal and Lowveld conditions. Do not confuse it with Sesbania punicea, the red-flowered invasive relative.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Sunn Hemp and the Waiting Soil
narration:
Sunn hemp is a fast annual option.

It can reach 2 metres in one season and adds roughly 100 to 165kg of nitrogen per hectare from its above-ground biomass alone.

After slashing and working it into the soil, do not expect the next crop to use that nitrogen at once.

Soil organisms need 2-6 weeks to break down the plant material and release nitrogen in a form roots can take up.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Where to Place Nitrogen Fixers
narration:
Place nitrogen fixers uphill or upwind of fruit trees, so fertility moves downhill towards the fruit trees.

In a food forest, plant nitrogen fixers at twice fruit-tree density early on.

As the canopy closes, thin the nitrogen fixers.

For a degraded field in a warm, moist KZN summer, Sesbania sesban is the practical fast annual choice.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Mulch Plants and Chop and Drop
narration:
Some plants grow deep, wide-ranging roots.

Those roots can draw up minerals that other crops cannot reach.

When you cut the plant and leave it on the ground, chop and drop returns that material to the surface.

This helps hold moisture, suppress weeds, and build steady organic matter, even when the exact fertility gain is debated.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: Chop and Drop
narration: Watch the cut leaves lying around living plants. They protect the soil surface, hold moisture, and slowly become organic matter as soil life breaks them down.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Choose the Right Comfrey
narration:
Comfrey is a classic mulch plant because of its deep roots.

Use Bocking 14 comfrey, Symphytum times uplandicum.

This cultivar is sterile and will not spread by seed.

Ordinary comfrey can set viable seed and spread beyond where you planted it, so the cultivar choice matters.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Work With Helpful Insects
narration:
Permaculture works with biology rather than sprays.

Ladybirds eat aphids, while wasps parasitise caterpillars.

Flowering plants such as African basil, borage, and marigold attract these pest-controlling insects.

They help build a living pest-control system around your crops that can strengthen every year.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Wild Garlic for Pest Control
narration:
Wild garlic, Tulbaghia violacea, is a strong guild plant for pest management.

Its sulphur compounds repel aphids and whitefly.

It is drought-tolerant, and Highveld frost-hardy once established.

It is edible and multiplies easily to share. Interplant it with African basil so flowering plants attract aphid predators like ladybirds.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: What Makes a Plant Guild
narration:
A plant guild is a group chosen to support one central tree, usually fruit or nut.

Each member has a job: fixing nitrogen, drawing up minerals, attracting beneficial insects, repelling pests, covering ground, or producing food.

The plants are selected as a community, not as separate crops.

Once established, a well-built guild needs little from you.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Watch: A Mango Guild
narration: Look at the central mango and the plants around it. Notice how the guild works as one team, with each plant supporting the tree in a different way.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Place and Cut the Sesbania
narration:
For a mango guild in KZN's Lowveld or coast, place Sesbania sesban on the north-east and north-west sides.

Cut it back yearly for nitrogen and mulch.

Cutting stops it shading and competing with the mango.

title: Reading the Landscape
narration:
A permaculture course for South African smallholder farmers.

title: Lesson 1: Where Rain Goes

title: Trace Contours with an A-Frame
narration:

title: Slow It High, Sink It Mid, Control It Low
narration:

title: Lesson 2: Read Sun and Shade
narration:

This helps you choose where to place tender crops, trees, buildings, and other parts of your farm.

title: Check Winter Shadows Before Building

title: Lesson 3: Read Wind, Frost, and Slope

title: Frost Flows Downhill
narration:

title: Choose Airflow and Warmth

title: Soil Health & Composting
narration:
Soil is more than the ground under your feet.

It is a living place that feeds crops, holds water, and carries your harvest.

title: Why This Matters
narration:
Years of monoculture, overgrazing, or stubble-burning leave soil that depends on bought fertiliser to produce anything.

When soil life is lost, the ground becomes pale, compacted, and difficult to farm.

Compost, mulch, cover crops, and worm farms can rebuild living soil on smallholder farms across South Africa.

narration:

title: Soil Is Alive
narration:
A teaspoon of good topsoil holds more organisms than there are people on Earth.

Bacteria and fungi process nutrients for plants.

Underground fungal threads move nutrients between plants. Worm channels are a visible sign of healthy topsoil.

Monoculture, overgrazing, and stubble-burning can strip this life away.

title: Watch: Look at the Soil
narration:
Compare the dark, living topsoil with the pale, compacted soil.

title: Test Your Soil with a Jar
narration:
Fill a jar one-third with soil, top it up with water, and add a drop of dish soap.

Shake the jar, then leave it to settle for a day.

Sand settles first, silt settles next, and clay stays suspended longest.

The layers show your soil texture without special equipment.

title: Read the Jar Layers
narration:
Thick sand at the bottom and cloudy, clay-tinted water on top means the soil is sandy.

Sandy soil drains fast and holds little water for roots.

Mulch heavily and add organic matter often.

This slows water loss and helps the soil hold moisture around growing plants.

title: Degraded Soil Can Recover
narration:
Pale, compacted soil with no worms and a sour smell is not simply a fixed soil type.

Continuous cropping, chemical use, or burning may have killed most of the soil life.

That is encouraging, because living soil can be rebuilt with compost, mulch, and gentler management.

title: Compost Feeds the Soil
narration:
Compost is organic matter that has decomposed.

It rebuilds soil structure and feeds the organisms that help plants grow.

A hot heap reaches usable compost in four to six weeks in warm, humid KZN.

On the cooler Highveld, it may take eight to twelve weeks.

title: Watch: Build the Compost Heap
narration:
Build the heap with dry browns and fresh greens.

Keep the layers moist, not wet, so air and decomposers can work.

title: Balance Browns and Greens
narration:
Layer 20 to 30cm of browns for every 5 to 10cm of greens.

Too much green material makes the heap wet, slimy, and ammonia-smelling.

Too much brown material keeps the heap cold for months.

The right balance gives the heap food, air, and enough heat to break down.

title: Keep the Compost Safe
narration:
Aim for a core temperature of 55 to 65°C.

This speeds decomposition and kills most weed seeds and pathogens.

Do not add meat, dairy, cooked scraps, diseased plants, or soil with persistent herbicide residue.

These materials can make the finished compost unsafe for the farm.

title: Keep Wattle Pods Out
narration:
Keep wattle seed pods out of the compost heap.

Their hard seed coat can survive ordinary composting heat and carry the plant into finished compost.

Wattle bark alone is safe to include, although it breaks down slowly.

Turn the heap every five to seven days and keep it moist, not wet.

title: Watch: Bare Soil and Mulch
narration:

title: Mulch Protects the Ground
narration:
Spread a 5 to 10cm layer of straw, dry grass, or wood chips over bare soil.

It also suppresses weeds and feeds soil life as it breaks down.

title: Cover Crops Between Seasons
narration:

title: Worm Farms Make Root Feed

title: Protect Soil All Year

Cover crops, mulch, and organic matter keep soil in place and help it stay alive.

title: Vegetables and Staple Crops
narration:
Welcome. This is Vegetables and Staple Crops. It's one of the ten modules in the ImbewuField training.

A productive garden is not the one that looks fullest on one day. It's the one that keeps food moving into the household, week after week.

In the next few minutes, we'll cover four things. How to build a bed. How to keep harvests coming. Which staples to grow. And what to do when pests arrive.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Why This Matters
narration:
Let's start with the problem.

One big sowing gives you a glut. Everything is ready at once. You eat what you can, you give some away, and the rest is wasted.

Then comes the gap. Nothing is ready. The garden is full of plants, but there's no food in it.

[pause]

Small sowings create a rhythm instead. Planting, tending and harvesting overlap. Something is always coming ready.

That rhythm is what feeds a household. Not the size of the garden.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Learning Outcomes
narration:
By the end of this module, you'll be able to make four decisions in your own field.

One. Build the right bed — matching the width and the bed type to your soil and your rainfall.

Two. Keep harvests moving, using succession planting and intercropping.

Three. Choose staples that protect you when one crop fails.

Four. Read a pest problem before you treat it.

[pause]

These four belong together. A well-shaped bed still fails if everything goes in on one day. A diverse planting still struggles if you treat every yellow leaf as an insect problem.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Roots Need Loose Soil, Paths Need Your Feet
narration:
Compacted soil loses its air spaces. Roots slow down. Water soaks in differently. The bed gets harder to work every season.

The protection is simple. Permanent paths, and a bed narrow enough to reach into from both sides.

One metre to one point two metres wide. That's the working number. At that width you can reach the centre from either path, and your feet never touch the growing area.

[pause]

Now think about your own beds. Can you reach the middle without stepping inside? Go and try it before you plant anything else.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Choose the Bed for the Soil and Rainfall
narration:
There's no single bed shape that's right everywhere.

Start with the least disturbance that solves your problem.

No-dig suits most garden soils. Leave the structure alone and build fertility on top.

Double-digging is hard work, and it should answer a real problem — compacted ground or heavy clay. Not habit.

Raised beds suit wet ground, where water needs somewhere to drain away to.

Sunken beds suit dry ground, where you want to catch and hold what rain you get.

[pause]

Look at your own ground after heavy rain. Does water sit, or does it run off? That answer chooses your bed.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Seed or Seedling?
narration:
Some crops resent having their roots disturbed. They do better sown straight where they'll grow. Beans, carrots and maize belong in that group.

Others do better with a protected start in a nursery, then transplanting. Tomatoes and brassicas belong there.

[pause]

Whichever you choose, spacing matters more than the packet suggests. Seed packets are printed for cooler, wetter places than most of South Africa. Give your plants more room than the smallest spacing on the packet.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Mark the Working Shape
narration:
Before you plant, mark the bed out.

One point two metres wide. Three metres long. One practice bed.

Use pegs and string. Mark the rectangle, and mark both access paths.

Then prepare for your own soil — no-dig first, and dig deeper only if your ground genuinely needs it.

[pause]

A string line turns an idea into a decision. Once the paths exist, keep them. Once the growing area exists, protect it.

That bed gets easier to improve every season, because you stopped walking on it.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: A Sowing Rhythm Keeps Food Moving
narration:
Succession planting is a calendar habit, not a special crop.

Choose something your household actually eats often. Then sow a small amount of it, again and again.

Plant a short row every two to three weeks.

[pause]

Less waste during a glut. Fresh food for longer. And the labour spreads out across the season instead of landing on you all at once.

If heat or heavy rain ruins one sowing, the others still carry the season.

Which fast crop could you sow in small batches? Decide on one, and start it this week.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Sow Little and Often
narration:
Here's what it looks like in practice.

Sow one. Then two to three weeks later, sow two. Then sow three. Then sow four.

By the time the fourth sowing is in the ground, the first is ready to harvest. The harvests begin to overlap.

[pause]

Two to three weeks is a starting rhythm, not a law. A cool-season leaf crop may hold longer. Heat may speed things up, or cause a failure.

Watch what your own garden does, and adjust the interval. That observation is the skill.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Each Crop Earns Its Place
narration:
Intercropping is not just crowding different plants together. Each plant needs a job, and enough space to do it.

The three sisters is the clearest example.

Maize gives height and structure.

Beans climb the maize, and store as protein.

Pumpkin spreads across the ground, shading the soil and holding moisture.

[pause]

Timing matters. Establish the maize first, so it's strong enough to carry the beans when they start to climb.

Three crops, one piece of ground, and none of them fighting the others.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Plan Backwards From Your Hungry Gap
narration:
Every place has a hungry gap. The weeks when the last harvest has run low and the next one isn't ready.

Yours might come after stored maize runs out. It might come before winter greens are ready. It might come in a dry period when water limits the garden.

[pause]

Don't copy somebody else's calendar. Name your own months first.

Write them down. Then choose the crop and the sowing date that puts food into that gap.

That's planning backwards, and it's the difference between a garden that looks productive and a household that eats.

title: Staples Are Food Insurance
narration:
A staple earns its place because it feeds the household beyond the day of harvest.

It carries energy or protein. It stores, or it stays in the ground until you need it. And often it carries cultural memory too.

[pause]

One staple leaves you vulnerable. Two or more give you options when weather or pests hit.

Grow at least two. Not one.

Which staple does your household rely on most heavily right now? That's the one whose failure would hurt most — so that's the one that needs a companion.

title: Different Staples Protect Against Different Risks
narration:
Each staple protects you against something different.

Maize gives calories, and stores dry. Open-pollinated maize also lets you save your own seed, if you manage isolation and selection.

Beans and cowpeas give a storable protein harvest.

Sweet potato tolerates dry periods, and its leaves are edible too.

Amadumbe handles wetter ground, where other staples struggle.

[pause]

Notice that they fail in different conditions. That's the whole point.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Diversity Keeps Food Moving
narration:
Resilience doesn't mean nothing fails.

It means one failure doesn't finish your household's food plan.

[pause]

One crop is one point of failure.

Two or more staples give you more ways to keep eating.

Different crops use water, soil and seasons differently. That difference is the protection.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Pests Are Messengers Before They Are Enemies
narration:
Pest pressure usually rises for a reason.

Plants under stress. One crop dominating the ground. Or broad chemical use that has already removed the predators that were helping you.

[pause]

So before you treat anything, look at the whole system.

Is the plant short of water? Is the soil compacted, or hungry? Are predators already working on the problem for you?

A yellow leaf is not automatically an insect. It can be water, nutrition, or root damage. Find out which before you act.
isiZulu_status: draft source reconciliation and first-language review required

title: Treat the Cause Before the Insect
narration:
Work through four steps, in order.

One. Observe. Look at the damage pattern, the underside of the leaf, the stem, and the plants nearby.

Two. Check for stress. Soil moisture, roots, spacing, nutrition, drainage.

Three. Protect what's helping you. Beneficial insects are doing work you'd otherwise do yourself.

Four. Only then, act — and start with the lightest thing that works. Physical removal and better plant health solve most small outbreaks.

[pause]

If you use a neem product, follow the label. Don't improvise a stronger mixture. Even lower-risk products harm the wrong insects when they're misused.

Be honest with yourself about which step you usually skip.

title: Field Assignment
narration:
Now the lesson finishes in the soil.

Build one bed that can keep feeding you. One point two metres by three metres.

Reach the middle from both sides. Keep every foot on the paths. Space your plants for your own climate. Mulch the bed.

[pause]

Give it a realistic minimum of ten days before you judge it.

Photograph it when it's planted. Then come back after ten days with what you observed.

The aim isn't a perfect picture. The aim is a bed whose shape, spacing and rhythm you chose on purpose.

title: Field Action
narration:
This week, put one bed into production.

One. Mark the bed and the paths.

Two. Plant, with your spacing and your sowing rhythm.

Three. Return after ten days, with a photo.

[pause]

Then observe. Adjust. And write it down.

Record the sowing date. The rain. What germinated. Pest pressure. What you harvested.

Season by season, your garden becomes less dependent on guesswork — and more on what you've actually seen happen on your own ground.

That record is worth more than any advice.

title: Water Harvesting
narration: Swales, berms, dams, rainwater tanks and greywater. Choose where to slow water, where it can soak in, and where excess water can leave safely.

title: Learning Outcomes
narration:
Find a level contour line before planning a swale.

Explain why a dam needs a designed spillway.

Follow roof water through a first-flush diverter and into a covered tank.

Keep greywater away from people and edible plant parts.

title: Swales Slow Water on the Slope
narration:
A swale is a level trench dug exactly on contour — not angled, perfectly level end to end — so water fills it evenly and soaks in rather than running off.

The excavated soil forms a berm on the downhill side.

Trees planted there draw on stored water long after the rain has stopped.

title: Watch: A Swale Sinks Water
narration:
A swale is a level trench on contour — it sinks water, it doesn't direct it.

[pause]

Water fills it evenly and soaks in rather than running off.

title: Plant on the Downhill Berm
narration:
The excavated soil forms a berm on the downhill side.

The berm, the downhill mound of excavated soil, is where you plant trees.

Trees planted there draw on stored water long after the rain has stopped.

title: Storms Need a Safe Overflow
narration:
A storm can bring more water than a swale can hold. Plan a stable overflow route before digging.

Trace it to a place that can receive the excess without erosion or harm. Do not simply send it towards a neighbour, road or building.

A second swale or dam is only an option if its capacity and overflow have also been checked.

title: Watch: The Overflow Point
narration:
Watch the upper swale fill. Excess water then follows the protected overflow route.

The diagram shows a connection to another basin. It does not give construction sizes. The receiving basin also needs a safe way to deal with excess water.

title: Know When Swales Fit the Slope
narration:
Slope alone does not tell you whether a swale is safe. Check soil depth, drainage, ground stability and what lies downhill.

Do not dig into steep, unstable or waterlogged ground on the strength of this diagram. Get a competent local practitioner to assess the site.

A small soil observation cannot prove that a large earthwork is safe.

title: Watch: Living Contour Barriers
narration:
This side view shows established grass barriers across a slope. Flow slows at the barriers and some soil settles above them.

[pause]

Grass barriers and terraces need their own site assessment. They are not an automatic fix for every steep slope. First mark and observe; agree on a suitable design before disturbing the ground.

title: Store Rain for the Dry Season
narration:
Stored water can help through dry periods. How long it lasts depends on rainfall, losses and how much you use.

Record when rain actually arrives on your site. A yearly rainfall total does not tell you how much water will be available in the driest month.

title: Design the Spillway Before the Wall
narration:
A dam wall holds water back. A spillway gives excess water a planned way around it.

Have a competent dam designer assess the catchment, soil, flood flows and downstream consequences before any wall is built. Check the approvals needed locally.

A bigger catchment also brings a bigger flood. Never build first and work out the spillway later.

title: Watch: Dam and Spillway

This explains the flow route. It is not a plan for constructing a dam. The spillway and its outlet must be designed for the site.

title: Keep the Dam Wall Clear
narration:
Keep trees and deep-rooted shrubs away from the dam wall, spillway and outlet. Their roots can damage these structures.

Maintain the protective grass cover and keep the spillway clear. Report erosion, cracks or unexpected seepage to a competent dam practitioner.

Do not dig out established roots from a dam wall yourself. Repairs need an assessed plan.

title: Your Roof Is a Harvesting Surface
narration:
Roof area, rainfall and collection losses determine potential harvest. Tank overflow and water use reduce what remains available.

For a calculation exercise, assume a 100 square metre roof, 800 millimetres of rain and a collection factor of 0.9. Multiply these to get 72,000 litres.

Those are example inputs, not a rainfall forecast or a promise that a garden will have enough water.

title: Divert the Dirty First Flush
narration:
Roof runoff can carry droppings, dust and other contamination. Divert the first runoff before it enters the tank.

The amount to divert depends on roof area and local conditions. Follow a suitable design and the device instructions; there is no single volume for every roof.

A first-flush diverter does not make water safe to drink.

title: Watch: First Flush to Tank
narration:
The first runoff fills the separate chamber. The float rises and closes it. Later runoff travels to the tank.

Later runoff is not necessarily safe drinking water. After the storm, drain and reset the diverter as its instructions require, away from edible crops.

title: Match Tank Size to the Dry Season
narration:
List the uses you want the tank to supply. Measure or estimate their daily demand.

Compare that demand with local rainfall records, usable storage and the dry period you need to cover.

A tank size on its own cannot tell you how many weeks it will last.

title: Keep Stored Water Protected
narration:
Keep the tank covered and screen openings against insects. Maintain the roof, gutters and diverter.

A filter alone does not guarantee safe drinking water. Drinking use needs suitable treatment, disinfection and water-quality checks with qualified advice.

Keep untreated water away from edible plant parts. Keep any alternative supply separate from drinking-water plumbing.

title: Greywater Is Washwater, Not Toilet Water
narration:
Greywater is used water from washing. Toilet water is different and must never enter this garden system.

Washwater can still carry germs, salts and cleaning products. Reuse depends on its source, quality and where it will go. Do not assume that clear-looking water is safe.

title: Keep Greywater Safe for Soil
narration:
Avoid water containing bleach, harsh cleaners or nappy waste. Do not reuse it when someone in the household is ill. Plain soap is not a guarantee of suitability.

Use suitable greywater promptly, within 24 hours. Stop if it ponds, smells or runs off.

Keep it below mulch, away from people and animals. Mulch does not disinfect water.

title: Watch: Greywater Under Mulch
narration:
Used basin water travels through a pipe to soil beneath mulch, away from the tree trunk. It soaks into the root zone.

[pause]

There is no spray and no contact with fruit. The water stays grey in the drawing because mulch does not make it safe to drink.

title: Use Greywater Only Where It Is Safe
narration:
Do not use greywater on leafy vegetables, root vegetables or seedlings.

A suitable system may supply established trees or non-edible plants while keeping water off edible parts. Get advice on water quality and stop if plants or soil show damage.

Check municipal requirements before fitting a permanent system. This lesson does not approve an installation.
